chapter: Cab Calloway, Lunceford, Hampton and Armstrong, 1941-45
title: Writing Armstrong into spots rather than blowing throughout
summary: McRae built a heavier band and spotted Armstrong in arrangements to rest his lip; Glaser objected until it worked in Canada.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong

Wilmington -- where they sent me to listen to the band. I took a -- what was going on with the band and with Louie. When I came back -- You must remember, I never worked with Louie until -- I never had any experience until he came to rehearsal that day after he came off his vacation with two weeks in Chicago. He had been out around Chicago on his vacation. Now Joe asked me to build him this band. So I got these different guys like Colt Bill Harrison -- put these musicians together -- it was pretty good. And you'll notice that, from his old arrangements, Louie played a lot more. He was blowing more. I figured that with all this brass I had behind him, I didn't want Louie to be killing

himself, you know, trying to blow over the top of this big band.
I had four trombones, four trumpets, or something like that. It was a heavier band than what he had before.
We wrote Louie in different. Put him in different spots like we did with Artie Shaw.
We didn't have Artie Shaw blowing all the way through the arrangements. We had him in spots, you know.

And when Joe came to rehearsal and heard the band, he figured that Louie wasn't playing enough, you know. Why -- because his previous band before, Louie was doing most of all the playing. It was just like he was trying to carry the whole thing.
And I thought maybe he was just killing himself, because it was just too much for him to be blowing over all this brass.
So we would write him in spots that would show him off better than him just standing up there blowing over the top of seven brass, or something like that -- all the rhythms and like that.

So my feelings was that Louie -- maybe his lips was going a little bit, you know, and he shouldn't be blowing that heavy, that much.
I think it was just too much for him to be --
So I say I'm gonna write him in different. (Inaudible) changing him in spots. Introductions, the band got the first chorus, Louie come in and play and then he comes back and play some more.

And then he ends up with Louie, you know. Make like a show thing. Like always Louie Armstrong there all the time -- all through the arrangements, but not blowing just over the top of the arrangements all the time like he was doing with the old band.
I noticed in some of the old things he was doing, he was just playing, you know, just blowing all the way straight through the arrangements.
So we started -- I started spotting him. Tell whoever wrote the arrangements, the ones that I did, the ones that -- Edgar Sampson would send out some
